stories.title: The 'National Park' That Stretches From Coast to Coast
stories.label: earth
stories.summary: A rewilding idea started on one ecologist's Pennsylvania property has grown into a nationwide movement to turn ordinary yards into a patchwork 'homegrown national park.' On his own land, wood thrushes have returned to nest and rare luna moths are showing up in record numbers, real proof that small changes add up. Thousands of people across the country have joined in, replacing lawns with native plants that feed birds, bees, and butterflies. It shows that you don't need a huge wilderness to help nature bounce back, just a shared shift in how we treat the land around us. The results are already visible, not just hoped for.
stories.why_good: It documents an actual, working conservation program with measurable ecological results, not a plan or study.

stories.title: 91-Year-Old 'Greybeard' Becomes Oldest Person to Hike the Appalachian Trail
stories.label: people
stories.summary: A 91-year-old man from Kentucky has just become the oldest person ever to hike the entire Appalachian Trail, all 2,190-plus miles of it. It took him 359 days and he took 71 falls along the way, but he kept getting back up and finishing what he started. He grew up in the Kentucky backwoods long before the trail even existed, and now his name is etched into hiking history. It's a wonderful reminder that age doesn't have to be a limit on big dreams.
stories.why_good: A real, completed personal achievement that shows resilience and possibility at any age, with no downside or controversy attached.

stories.title: Humanity's 3rd Visit to Mercury Kicks Off with the Successful Arrival of BepiColombo Mission
stories.label: space
stories.summary: A spacecraft called BepiColombo has successfully arrived at Mercury, only the third mission ever to reach our solar system's innermost planet. It's a joint project between European and Japanese space agencies, and getting there took years of careful looping around the sun to slow down enough to be captured by Mercury's gravity. Scientists are thrilled because Mercury is still one of the least understood planets, and this mission should teach us a lot about how it formed. It's a reminder of how much patient, careful engineering it takes to explore even our closest planetary neighbors. No explosions, no drama, just years of hard work paying off exactly as planned.
stories.why_good: A genuine scientific achievement that actually happened, expanding human knowledge peacefully and without controversy.
